The host-side world used to generate the Rust bindings. It deliberately
contains nothing else: the runner links WASI separately through
`wasmtime_wasi::p3::add_to_linker`, so this world only describes the
custom host import.
The world a layout strategy plugin compiles against.

The host-side world used to generate the Rust bindings. Like the other
tina imports, it holds only the custom interface; WASI is linked
separately through `wasmtime_wasi::p3::add_to_linker`.

The host-side world used to generate the Rust bindings. Like
`tina:http`'s, it holds only the custom import; WASI is linked
separately through `wasmtime_wasi::p3::add_to_linker`.

One engine-shaped probe: WASI (filesystem preopens, environment, stdout,
clocks, random) plus the tina:http host import, run by the case runner's
protocol (result-collector in, tested-module out).

The full tina TUI as one component (Option 2): the engine's host-import
set (http, plugin-host, policy, process) plus the host-owned tty
authority and the crash channel, over the standard run export the
packaged host drives by default. Same toolchain package as the engine
world (witgen takes one root package per tree); the identity that
matters is the component's imports/exports, not this local name.

The `wasi:http/service` world captures a broad category of HTTP services
including web applications, API servers, and proxies. It may be `include`d
in more specific worlds such as `wasi:http/middleware`.

The `wasi:http/middleware` world captures HTTP services that forward HTTP
Requests to another handler.

Components may implement this world to allow them to participate in handler
"chains" where a `request` flows through handlers on its way to some terminal
`service` and corresponding `response` flows in the opposite direction.

Issue `req`. The domain allowlist is evaluated before anything is
sent: an allowed domain completes when the response head is
available (see `sent`); an unknown domain returns an approval
request the engine must answer.

Answer a parked approval. `allow` sends the parked request now and
reports the outcome; anything else refuses it.

The layout contract vocabulary: tina_layout's GridSpec and solution
types as structured records (see tina docs/layout-plugin.md). The
record shapes are the single serialization - the same field names
serve the Dart codec (LayoutWire), the guest bindings and the host's
Val records. Plugins never change what a rectangle is.

Solve one spec for one terminal size. Synchronous; the host runs it
under an epoch deadline and falls back to the built-in solver on
any failure.

What a layout strategy plugin exports. Pure function, zero
capabilities: a strategy imports nothing beyond WASI and the contract's
own types (the host admits nothing else).
The mounted strategy, or none. Cheap enough to poll.

The host-mediated bridge the TUI imports. The host routes solve calls
to the mounted strategy plugin's own Store; components never call
components.

Invoke the configured plugin against immutable session context. The host
must not re-enter the suspended Tina engine Store while handling this call.
Revoke the lease and retire only its plugin Store.

Host-mediated lifecycle for one configured guest AgentPlugin. The lease is
issued by the host on open and is scoped to that plugin Store instance.

Widen the live policy with one entry after an approved escalation.
Validated fail-closed; the error carries the refusal. The engine
persists the grant itself - the host's widening is memory for this
run only.
The effective document for diagnostics and parity assertions.

Get the POSIX-style environment variables.

Each environment variable is provided as a pair of string variable names
and string value.

Morally, these are a value import, but until value imports are available
in the component model, this import function should return the same
values each time it is called.
Get the POSIX-style arguments to the program.

Return a path that programs should use as their initial current working
directory, interpreting `.` as shorthand for this.
Exit the current instance and any linked instances.

Exit the current instance and any linked instances, reporting the
specified status code to the host.

The meaning of the code depends on the context, with 0 usually meaning
"success", and other values indicating various types of failure.

This function does not return; the effect is analogous to a trap, but
without the connotation that something bad has happened.
Run the program.

Return a stream for reading from stdin.

This function returns a stream which provides data read from stdin,
and a future to signal read results.

If the stream's readable end is dropped the future will resolve to success.

If the stream's writable end is dropped the future will either resolve to
success if stdin was closed by the writer or to an error-code if reading
failed for some other reason.

Multiple streams may be active at the same time. The behavior of concurrent
reads is implementation-specific.

Write the given stream to stdout.

If the stream's writable end is dropped this function will either return
success once the entire contents of the stream have been written or an
error-code representing a failure.

Otherwise if there is an error the readable end of the stream will be
dropped and this function will return an error-code.

Write the given stream to stderr.

If the stream's writable end is dropped this function will either return
success once the entire contents of the stream have been written or an
error-code representing a failure.

Otherwise if there is an error the readable end of the stream will be
dropped and this function will return an error-code.

Terminal input.

In the future, this may include functions for disabling echoing,
disabling input buffering so that keyboard events are sent through
immediately, querying supported features, and so on.

Terminal output.

In the future, this may include functions for querying the terminal
size, being notified of terminal size changes, querying supported
features, and so on.

If stdin is connected to a terminal, return a `terminal-input` handle
allowing further interaction with it.

An interface providing an optional `terminal-input` for stdin as a
link-time authority.

If stdout is connected to a terminal, return a `terminal-output` handle
allowing further interaction with it.

An interface providing an optional `terminal-output` for stdout as a
link-time authority.

If stderr is connected to a terminal, return a `terminal-output` handle
allowing further interaction with it.

An interface providing an optional `terminal-output` for stderr as a
link-time authority.

Ask the host to run `req`. The host evaluates its capability rules
(and the optional backstop profile) before any process exists:
allow starts the child, deny refuses with the rule, ask (or no
match) returns an approval request the engine must answer.

Answer an approval request. `allow` spawns now and reports
`started`; anything else refuses the spawn.

Resolve when the process exits, and reap it. Every started
process is eventually waited.
Terminate the process (SIGKILL on POSIX hosts). Idempotent.

The host's tty authority: it owns the real terminal, so window size is a
live answer (re-supplied on resize), not an env snapshot.

The guest-to-host failure channel (spike finding 4): a guest Dart
exception that would otherwise kill the guest task and park the host's
`run` call forever calls `fail` first (from the top-level zone guard),
then invokes the WASI `exit` import as the structural backstop. The host
records the message, stops waiting, restores the terminal and reports
`guest crashed: <message>` with a non-zero exit.

Construct an empty HTTP Fields.

The resulting `fields` is mutable.

Construct an HTTP Fields.

The resulting `fields` is mutable.

The list represents each name-value pair in the Fields. Names
which have multiple values are represented by multiple entries in this
list with the same name.

The tuple is a pair of the field name, represented as a string, and
Value, represented as a list of bytes. In a valid Fields, all names
and values are valid UTF-8 strings. However, values are not always
well-formed, so they are represented as a raw list of bytes.

An error result will be returned if any header or value was
syntactically invalid, if a header was forbidden, or if the
entries would exceed an implementation size limit.

Get all of the values corresponding to a name. If the name is not present
in this `fields`, an empty list is returned. However, if the name is
present but empty, this is represented by a list with one or more
empty field-values present.

Returns `true` when the name is present in this `fields`. If the name is
syntactically invalid, `false` is returned.

Set all of the values for a name. Clears any existing values for that
name, if they have been set.

Fails with `header-error.immutable` if the `fields` are immutable.

Fails with `header-error.size-exceeded` if the name or values would
exceed an implementation-defined size limit.

Delete all values for a name. Does nothing if no values for the name
exist.

Fails with `header-error.immutable` if the `fields` are immutable.

Delete all values for a name. Does nothing if no values for the name
exist.

Returns all values previously corresponding to the name, if any.

Fails with `header-error.immutable` if the `fields` are immutable.

Append a value for a name. Does not change or delete any existing
values for that name.

Fails with `header-error.immutable` if the `fields` are immutable.

Fails with `header-error.size-exceeded` if the value would exceed
an implementation-defined size limit.

Retrieve the full set of names and values in the Fields. Like the
constructor, the list represents each name-value pair.

The outer list represents each name-value pair in the Fields. Names
which have multiple values are represented by multiple entries in this
list with the same name.

The names and values are always returned in the original casing and in
the order in which they will be serialized for transport.

Make a deep copy of the Fields. Equivalent in behavior to calling the
`fields` constructor on the return value of `copy-all`. The resulting

Construct a new `request` with a default `method` of `GET`, and
`none` values for `path-with-query`, `scheme`, and `authority`.

`headers` is the HTTP Headers for the Request.

`contents` is the optional body content stream with `none`
representing a zero-length content stream.
Once it is closed, `trailers` future must resolve to a result.
If `trailers` resolves to an error, underlying connection
will be closed immediately.

`options` is optional `request-options` resource to be used
if the request is sent over a network connection.

It is possible to construct, or manipulate with the accessor functions
below, a `request` with an invalid combination of `scheme`
and `authority`, or `headers` which are not permitted to be sent.
It is the obligation of the `handler.handle` implementation
to reject invalid constructions of `request`.

The returned future resolves to result of transmission of this request.

Get the HTTP Related Scheme for the Request. When `none`, the

Set the HTTP Related Scheme for the Request. When `none`, the

Get the authority of the Request's target URI. A value of `none` may be used

HTTPS schemes always require an authority.

Set the authority of the Request's target URI. A value of `none` may be used

This interface defines all of the types and methods for implementing HTTP
Requests and Responses, as well as their headers, trailers, and bodies.

This function may be called with either an incoming request read from the
network or a request synthesized or forwarded by another component.

This interface defines a handler of HTTP Requests.

In a `wasi:http/service` this interface is exported to respond to an
incoming HTTP Request with a Response.

In `wasi:http/middleware` this interface is both exported and imported as
the "downstream" and "upstream" directions of the middleware chain.

This function may be used to either send an outgoing request over the
network or to forward it to another component.

This interface defines an HTTP client for sending "outgoing" requests.

Most components are expected to import this interface to provide the
capability to send HTTP requests to arbitrary destinations on a network.

The type signature of `client.send` is the same as `handler.handle`. This
duplication is currently necessary because some Component Model tooling
(including WIT itself) is unable to represent a component importing two
instances of the same interface. A `client.send` import may be linked
directly to a `handler.handle` export to bypass the network.

One outgoing request. `method` is `GET` or `POST` (upper-case, as
`dart:io` sends it); `url` is absolute; `body` is the request body
or none for GET.

The response before its body: status code plus header pairs. Header
names keep the case the server sent.

An approval the domain allowlist parked: nothing is sent until the
engine answers `respond`. `url` is the request's absolute URL.

Why a request failed before any body: a host-side message, never a
raw OS error, so guests can surface it verbatim.

A request the host sent: the head (status + headers), the body as
a byte stream, in order, chunked as the network delivers it, and
a future that resolves with an error when the body transfer
failed, and successfully once every body byte was delivered.
Dropping the stream cancels the transfer.

This is a catch-all error for anything that doesn't fit cleanly into a
more specific case. It also includes an optional string for an
unstructured description of the error. Users should not depend on the
string for diagnosing errors, as it's not required to be consistent

These cases are inspired by the IANA HTTP Proxy Error Types:

Field names are always strings.

Field names should always be treated as case insensitive by the `fields`
resource for the purposes of equality checking.

Field values should always be ASCII strings. However, in
reality, HTTP implementations often have to interpret malformed values,
so they are provided as a list of bytes.

This following block defines the `fields` resource which corresponds to
HTTP standard Fields. Fields are a common representation used for both
Headers and Trailers.

A `fields` may be mutable or immutable. A `fields` created using the
constructor, `from-list`, or `clone` will be mutable, but a `fields`
resource given by other means (including, but not limited to,
`request.headers`) might be be immutable. In an immutable fields, the
`set`, `append`, and `delete` operations will fail with
`header-error.immutable`.

A `fields` resource should store `field-name`s and `field-value`s in their
original casing used to construct or mutate the `fields` resource. The `fields`
resource should use that original casing when serializing the fields for
transport or when returning them from a method.

Implementations may impose limits on individual field values and on total
aggregate field section size. Operations that would exceed these limits
fail with `header-error.size-exceeded`

The `tina:http` host interface: the engine's HTTP port
(`tina_core.HttpClientPort`) served by the host instead of `dart:io`.

The host enforces the capability document it was launched with
(`docs/capability_merger.md`): the network domain entries are the
allowlist. A request to an allowed domain proceeds; an unknown domain
returns an approval request the engine answers with `respond` after
its approval flow - the same round-trip `tina:process` uses, because
the host cannot call back into a blocked guest. `widen` (the
`tina:policy` interface) makes a remembered domain grant stick for the
rest of the run.

One function covers the port's POST and GET: the method travels in the
request. The response head (status + headers) arrives first; the body
is a component-model byte stream the guest reads incrementally, paired
with a future resolving once the whole body has been delivered - the
same shape as `wasi:cli/stdin.read-via-stream`, so guests lower it
with the stream/future machinery they already use for stdio.

1.1.0: `send` returns an outcome (`sent` / `approval` / `denied`) and
`respond` answers an approval, mirroring `tina:process@1.1.0`.

The `tina:policy` host interface: the escalation channel of the
capability merger (`docs/capability_merger.md`).

The engine compiles the capability document and the host enforces it.
When an approval flow grants more than one call - an "always" or
scoped answer - the engine persists the grant through its own stores
and calls `widen` here so the host's live policy covers later calls
without re-asking. Entries are validated fail-closed (patterns
compile, directories exist, protected paths are never covered); a
widened directory is recorded for the engine's gating but cannot add a
preopen - those are fixed at instantiation and take effect on the next
launch.

`snapshot` exposes the effective document (launch entries plus
widenings) for diagnostics and parity assertions.

The `tina:process` host interface: the engine's process port
(`tina_core.ProcessPort`) served by the host, because WASI has no
process spawn. Spec: docs/tina_process.md.

The host enforces the capability document it was launched with
(`docs/capability_merger.md`): the command rules are host-held, so an
engine compiled from a different policy cannot widen itself by editing
what travels with the request. A request may still carry an access
profile as a fail-closed backstop assertion: deny beats ask beats
allow. An `ask` verdict returns to the engine as an approval request it
answers with `respond` - the host cannot call back into a blocked
guest.

1.1.0: the per-request profile became optional (the host-held capability
rules are the authority); the verdict semantics are unchanged.
